The consignment weighed 112 tons in total and was valued at 8,400 pounds sterling. The Andromache was a vessel of 598 tons register sailing under Captain Ruiz, and she was expected to complete the passage in eleven days; however, the journey was delayed when calms off Cape St. Vincent held her up for four days. The cargo was insured at Lloyd's, with the premium written at one and three-quarters percent. In Swansea, the company's agents, Morris and Sons, were instructed that no ingot was to be sold below 64 pounds per ton. Of the 1,240 ingots shipped, 300 bore the company mark of 1887, while the remaining 940 carried the mark of 1888. Additionally, two ingots were set aside at Huelva to serve as assay samples and were not placed aboard the ship.

The Toledo express train was running twenty minutes behind schedule and was traveling at an estimated speed of 45 miles per hour when it struck a stationary freight train. The freight train had been shunted onto the main line, which placed it in the express's path.

The collision resulted in two deaths: the engineer of the express, Michael O'Hara, and the fireman. In addition, nine passengers were injured, though none of the injuries proved fatal.

An investigating board examined the accident and determined its cause. The board found that James Caldwell, the station agent at Oberlin, had failed to deliver the order that fixed a meeting point at Elyria.

The express train itself consisted of five vehicles: a locomotive, a baggage car, two coaches, and a sleeper. According to the conductor's count taken at Cleveland, there were 61 passengers aboard the train.

The damage to the rolling stock was assessed at a cost of 14,200 dollars.

Following its investigation, the board made two recommendations. The first was that the block signal system be introduced over the whole division, and the second was that Caldwell be dismissed from his position. The company carried out both of these recommendations within the year.

On 28 May 1888, the Rio Tinto Copper Company shipped a consignment of 1,240 ingots of refined copper from Huelva, sending them aboard the sailing barque Andromache on a voyage bound for Swansea. The copper ingots together weighed 112 tons and were valued at 8,400 pounds sterling.

The Andromache itself was a vessel of 598 tons register, sailing under the command of Captain Ruiz. The ship's captain expected the passage to take eleven days, but the voyage was held up by calm conditions off Cape St. Vincent, which delayed the vessel for four days.

Insurance covering the cargo was written at Lloyd's, with a premium of one and three-quarters percent.

In Swansea, the company's agents were Morris and Sons, and they were instructed that no ingot was to be sold below a price of 64 pounds per ton.

Of the 1,240 ingots in the shipment, 300 carried the company's mark of 1887, while the remainder bore the mark of 1888. Separately, two ingots were set aside at Huelva to serve as assay samples, and these two were not shipped with the rest of the cargo.
